Chapter 195

Calcium Channel Blockers

Tintinalli Ch.195 — Section 15 Toxicology

Clifford P. Masom, Christian Tomaszewski

🇹🇭 Thai EM Board📗 Rosen's

Introduction: Clinical Uses and Epidemiology

Calcium channel blockers are used for hypertension, angina, rate control of supraventricular dysrhythmias, migraine prophylaxis, Raynaud-related vasospasm, and esophageal spasm. Toxicity is dangerous because the therapeutic target is the same physiology required for perfusion: calcium entry through L-type channels in myocardium, conduction tissue, vascular smooth muscle, and pancreatic beta cells.

Board framing: the poisoned patient usually declares toxicity as hypotension, bradycardia or conduction delay, shock, and hyperglycemia. Treat the physiology early; do not wait for a serum CCB level.
  • All three CCB classes increase coronary blood flow in a dose-dependent fashion
  • Verapamil is the most potent negative inotrope of all CCBs
  • Extended-release (ER) formulations complicate overdose management by delaying toxicity onset to 6-12 hours or longer after ingestion
  • Children are particularly sensitive to CCB toxicity; deaths have been reported after even single-tablet ingestion
  • Adults receiving long-term therapy can develop toxicity from as little as twice their regular daily dose

Pharmacology: L-type Calcium Channels and Drug Classes

CCBs bind the alpha-1 subunit of the L-type calcium channel and favor the closed or inactivated channel state. The result is decreased calcium influx, impaired myocardial contraction, slowed SA/AV nodal conduction, arterial vasodilation, and reduced insulin release. In overdose, selectivity is lost and all classes can produce both vasodilatory and myocardial shock.

Major Drug Classes

  • Phenylalkylamines: verapamil; strongest negative inotropy and nodal depression.
  • Benzothiazepines: diltiazem; nodal slowing with less myocardial depression than verapamil.
  • Dihydropyridines: nifedipine, amlodipine, nicardipine, felodipine, isradipine, nimodipine, nisoldipine; relatively more vascular selective at therapeutic doses.

Verapamil, nifedipine, and diltiazem have relatively short serum half-lives in immediate-release form, but extended-release products are common. ER ingestion can delay onset of toxicity for 6 to 12 hours or longer and can prolong shock through ongoing absorption.

Tintinalli source check

Table 195-1

Use this table while comparing CCB classes, half-lives, maximum adult daily doses, and why verapamil behaves as the most cardiodepressant agent.

Exam trap: dihydropyridines may cause reflex tachycardia at therapeutic doses, but large overdoses can still cause bradycardia, conduction delay, myocardial depression, and profound hypotension.

Hyperglycemia is a useful clinical clue. CCBs inhibit calcium-mediated insulin release from pancreatic beta cells; more severe hyperglycemia generally tracks with more severe poisoning and helps distinguish CCB toxicity from beta-blocker poisoning, where hypoglycemia may occur.

Because calcium influx is necessary for insulin release and myocardial carbohydrate use, severe CCB poisoning creates a double problem: poor contractility and impaired cellular fuel handling. This is the rationale for early high-dose insulin therapy in refractory shock.

Clinical Features: Toxicity Presentation and Systemic Effects

The dominant life threats are cardiovascular: hypotension from decreased cardiac output and peripheral vasodilation, bradycardia, AV block, junctional rhythm, ventricular escape rhythms, and cardiovascular collapse. Verapamil and diltiazem more often produce bradycardia and conduction block, while dihydropyridines more often begin with vasodilatory hypotension.

Clinical severity depends on the agent, formulation, dose, coingestants, patient age, and baseline cardiovascular reserve. Adults on chronic therapy may become toxic after only modest dose escalation; children can deteriorate after small ingestions, including single-tablet exposures.

  • Pulmonary and CNS effects are generally secondary to decreased myocardial function and impaired organ perfusion
  • Cardiogenic pulmonary edema is sometimes observed in severe overdoses, especially if large volumes of crystalloid are infused during resuscitation
  • Acute lung injury (noncardiogenic pulmonary edema) has also been reported
  • Seizures, delirium, stroke, and coma have been described and are presumed to be secondary to cerebral hypoperfusion
  • Alteration in consciousness in the absence of hypotension should not be attributed to CCB toxicity; evaluate for other causes of mental status alteration
  • Nausea and vomiting are common
  • Life-threatening GI complications include bowel necrosis and ischemia, even without hypotension
  • ER products can cause development of bezoars
Do not anchor on mental status alone: coma, seizure, delirium, or stroke-like findings may reflect hypoperfusion, but altered consciousness without hypotension should trigger evaluation for other toxins and neurologic causes.

Diagnosis: Clinical Assessment, ECG, and Laboratory Findings

Diagnosis is clinical and should be suspected in any patient with bradycardia, AV block, hypotension, hyperglycemia, or shock after possible access to CCBs. Obtain the exact product name and formulation whenever possible because ER preparations drive observation time and decontamination decisions.

Initial evaluation should include continuous cardiac monitoring, 12-lead ECG, glucose, electrolytes, renal function, calcium, magnesium, phosphorus, venous blood gas, lactate, and targeted drug levels when the history suggests coingestion, especially digoxin.

ECG findings range from sinus bradycardia to varying degrees of AV block and intraventricular conduction delay. Hyperkalemia, myocardial ischemia, hypothermia, clonidine-like alpha-2 agonist poisoning, cardiac glycosides, beta-blockers, antiarrhythmics, and sedative-hypnotics are key mimics.

  • Systemic hypoperfusion may cause a lactic acidosis with elevated anion gap and low serum bicarbonate level
  • Hypokalemia may be observed in severe overdoses
  • Serum calcium levels are usually normal
  • Ionized serum calcium levels may be followed during treatment with IV calcium preparations
  • The optimum serum calcium level for patients with severe CCB poisoning is unknown
  • CCB serum concentrations are not routinely available and are not used in management
  • Screen blood and urine for other potential toxins after suicidal overdose
Reference anchor: Tintinalli Table 195-2 lists the differential for bradycardia, AV block, and hypotension; keep it beside beta-blocker and digoxin toxicity in board preparation.

Table 195-2

Place this next to the diagnosis section because the board stem often gives bradycardia plus hypotension before revealing the ingestion.

Practical point: serum CCB concentrations are not routinely available and are not used to guide emergency treatment. Resuscitation is driven by perfusion, ECG, glucose, lactate, and response to therapy.

Management: Calcium, Glucagon, High-Dose Insulin, Vasopressors, Lipid Emulsion, ECMO

Start with resuscitation, airway assessment, IV access, continuous ECG monitoring, frequent blood pressure checks, and early toxicology or poison center consultation. Treat hypotension aggressively but reassess after each intervention because excessive crystalloid can worsen pulmonary edema.

Initial treatment sequence: stabilize airway and circulation, give crystalloid if appropriate, administer IV calcium, add vasopressors for shock, and begin high-dose insulin early when myocardial depression or refractory hypotension is present.

GI Decontamination

  • Activated charcoal is reasonable after significant immediate-release or extended-release ingestion if the airway is protected.
  • Multidose activated charcoal is mainly considered for ER preparations.
  • Whole-bowel irrigation may be used for large ER ingestions, with close monitoring because unstable patients may not tolerate it.
  • Ipecac and routine gastric lavage are not recommended.
Calcium: calcium gluconate 10% 30 mL IV or calcium chloride 10% 10 mL IV may be repeated. Calcium chloride supplies more elemental calcium but is more caustic, so central access is preferred when available.
Vasopressors: no single agent is universally superior. Epinephrine or norepinephrine is commonly used and titrated to a perfusion target; multiple agents may be required in severe mixed vasodilatory and cardiogenic shock.
High-dose insulin: give regular insulin 1 unit/kg IV bolus, then start 1 unit/kg/h with dextrose support. Titrate up to 10 units/kg/h by hemodynamic response while monitoring glucose and potassium closely.
Tintinalli source check

Table 195-4

Keep this directly under HDI dosing because it contains the glucose, insulin, dextrose, potassium, and titration protocol that students actually need during question review.

Glucagon: may improve hemodynamics in some CCB cases and is especially considered when bradycardia or beta-blocker coingestion is possible, but it is not the definitive therapy for refractory CCB shock.
Pacing: transcutaneous or transvenous pacing can improve severe bradycardia but may not correct hypotension when vasodilation and poor contractility dominate.
Lipid emulsion: consider as rescue therapy for refractory shock, especially with lipophilic CCBs. Monitor for complications and avoid letting lipid delay definitive extracorporeal support when shock is worsening.
ECMO/extracorporeal support: consult early for persistent shock despite calcium, vasopressors, high-dose insulin, and rescue measures. Tintinalli emphasizes ECMO as the preferred rescue pathway when available.

📗 Rosen's EM 10th Edition — Comprehensive CCB Toxicity Management

Rosen's reinforces an early multimodal approach: aggressive supportive care, calcium, vasopressors, high-dose insulin, careful decontamination for extended-release products, and escalation to lipid therapy or ECMO when shock is refractory. It also stresses the same class distinction: non-dihydropyridines are more nodal/myocardial, while dihydropyridines are more vasodilatory at therapeutic doses.

  • Emphasizes importance of recognizing severe CCB toxicity and initiating aggressive supportive care early
  • Details pharmacologic differences between dihydropyridines (peripheral vascular-selective) and non-dihydropyridines (direct nodal effects)
  • Highlights hyperglycemia as a distinguishing feature of CCB toxicity versus β-blocker toxicity
  • Provides comprehensive calcium dosing protocols with emphasis on central line placement for calcium chloride
  • Covers high-dose insulin therapy as a proven rescue therapy with detailed dosing and monitoring protocols
  • Discusses vasopressor selection (epinephrine, norepinephrine preferred for combined alpha and beta effects)
  • Emphasizes role of transcutaneous and transvenous pacing for symptomatic bradycardia
  • Covers lipid emulsion and ECMO as rescue therapies in profound cardiogenic shock
  • Details importance of GI decontamination with activated charcoal and whole-bowel irrigation for ER formulations
  • Addresses disposition: IR formulations—6-hour observation; ER formulations—12-24 hour observation minimum

Drug Dose Reference

Initial Stabilization

  • Crystalloid: 20 mL/kg IV; repeat if needed while watching for pulmonary edema.
  • Atropine/pacing may be used for bradycardia, but response is often limited in severe CCB poisoning.

Calcium Salts

  • Calcium gluconate 10%: 30 mL IV; may repeat.
  • Calcium chloride 10%: 10 mL IV; may repeat, preferably through a central line.
  • Monitor ionized calcium and avoid clinically significant hypercalcemia.

High-Dose Insulin

  • Regular insulin bolus: 1 unit/kg IV.
  • Infusion: start 1 unit/kg/h with dextrose support; titrate up to 10 units/kg/h to hemodynamic goal.
  • Check glucose every 15-20 minutes and monitor potassium closely.

Vasopressors and Glucagon

  • Epinephrine or norepinephrine: 1-5 micrograms/min, titrated to effect.
  • Glucagon: 5 mg IV for bradycardia/hypotension; may repeat.

Rescue Therapies

  • 20% lipid emulsion: 1.5 mL/kg IV bolus, then 0.25 mL/kg/min infusion when used as rescue therapy.
  • Extracorporeal blood pressure support/ECMO is considered when refractory shock persists despite medical therapy.

Dose source: Tintinalli's Emergency Medicine 9th Ed, Chapter 195, Table 195-3, Table 195-4, and Figure 195-1, p.1277-1278. Confirm with a toxicologist or poison center for real patient care.

Disposition and Follow-up

Patients with altered mental status, bradycardia, conduction delay, hypotension, metabolic instability, or need for antidotal/vasoactive therapy require ICU-level monitoring. Disposition should account for formulation, dose, time since ingestion, coingestants, and social/suicide risk.

Observation rule: asymptomatic immediate-release ingestions with normal vital signs and ECG are generally observed for at least 6 hours; potentially toxic extended-release ingestions need at least 24 hours of monitoring.
  • IR formulations: 6-hour observation period adequate for asymptomatic patients with normal vitals and ECG
  • ER formulations: 12-24 hour minimum observation period required due to delayed absorption and prolonged toxicity
  • Extended-release preparation warrants admission and monitoring for delayed toxicity development
  • Patients requiring hospitalization: Those with altered mental status, bradycardia, conduction delays, or hypotension require ICU admission
  • Contact poison control for guidance on specific ingestions

Key Clinical Pearls: CCB Toxicity Summary

CCB toxicity causes bradycardia, hypotension, AV conduction delays, and potential life-threatening cardiogenic shock; severity is unpredictable, particularly with non-dihydropyridine agents (verapamil most lethal)
HYPERGLYCEMIA (NOT hypoglycemia) is a CHARACTERISTIC and POOR PROGNOSTIC finding in CCB toxicity; this distinguishes CCB poisoning from β-blocker toxicity, which typically causes euglycemia or hypoglycemia
Calcium chloride or calcium gluconate is the first-line antidote: Use calcium chloride 1 g IV rapid push via CENTRAL LINE (preferred; contains 270 mg elemental Ca per gram) or calcium gluconate 3 g IV via peripheral line (contains 90 mg elemental Ca per gram); repeat dosing every 10-20 minutes as needed or continuous infusion 2-6 g/hour
Atropine is OFTEN INEFFECTIVE for CCB-induced bradycardia; transcutaneous or transvenous pacing may be needed for symptomatic bradycardia unresponsive to other therapy
HIGH-DOSE INSULIN EUGLYCEMIA THERAPY (HIET) is highly effective for refractory hypotension and bradycardia: Begin 1 unit/kg IV bolus, then 1-10 units/kg/hour infusion with dextrose to maintain glucose 100-200 mg/dL; response expected within 15-30 minutes; can be used simultaneously with calcium and vasopressors
Vasopressors (epinephrine, norepinephrine titrated to MAP ≥65 mmHg) are frequently required to maintain perfusion pressure after calcium administration
Non-dihydropyridines (verapamil, diltiazem) are significantly more cardiotoxic than dihydropyridines; verapamil is the most lethal CCB, causing more deaths than all other CCBs combined
Dihydropyridines (nifedipine, amlodipine) cause peripheral vasodilation with reflex tachycardia at therapeutic doses due to vascular selectivity; lose selectivity and may cause bradycardia in severe overdose
Lipid emulsion therapy has been successfully used in severe, refractory cases unresponsive to calcium, glucagon, and vasopressors; provides pharmacologic 'sink' for fat-soluble drugs and improves cardiac substrate availability
ECMO should be considered for profound cardiogenic shock unresponsive to all medical therapies (calcium, insulin, vasopressors, lipid emulsion); contact ECMO team before starting lipid therapy if ECMO is planned
Extended-release formulations delay toxicity onset; observe for 12-24 hours minimum; continuous absorption can cause biphasic or recurrent toxicity requiring repeated doses of antidotes
Whole-bowel irrigation with polyethylene glycol should be considered for massive sustained-release ingestions
All pediatric CCB ingestions warrant medical observation and admission; deaths reported after single-tablet ingestion in children
Patients on chronic CCB therapy can develop toxicity from doses as little as twice their regular daily dose

Inline Assessment MCQs

Q1. A 54-year-old man intentionally ingests 3600 mg of extended-release diltiazem. On presentation: HR 42 bpm, BP 78/50 mmHg, normal mental status, blood glucose 245 mg/dL. What is the most important early intervention?
  • A. Insulin with dextrose for hyperglycemia
  • B. High-dose IV calcium gluconate 15-30 mL of 10% solution repeated as needed
  • C. Atropine 1 mg IV for bradycardia
  • D. Observation alone; diltiazem toxicity is usually self-limited
Calcium is the first-line treatment for CCB toxicity. High-dose IV calcium should be given early and aggressively. This patient has severe bradycardia and hypotension from diltiazem (a non-dihydropyridine with strong cardiac effects). Calcium gluconate (peripheral line safe) or calcium chloride (central line; preferred) should be initiated immediately. The hyperglycemia is typical of CCB toxicity (from inhibited insulin secretion) and requires less urgent intervention than the cardiogenic shock.
Q2. A 48-year-old woman with verapamil toxicity has received 2 doses of calcium gluconate without improvement in her heart rate (now 38 bpm) and blood pressure (now 65/35 mmHg). What is the most appropriate next intervention?
  • A. Repeat calcium doses every 15-20 minutes until response
  • B. Administer atropine 2-3 mg IV for bradycardia
  • C. Initiate transcutaneous pacing and call for ECMO
  • D. Start high-dose insulin (1 unit/kg) with dextrose infusion in combination with calcium and vasopressors
After initial calcium therapy without adequate response, high-dose insulin therapy with dextrose should be initiated. HIET works through different mechanisms than calcium (improved intracellular calcium handling and substrate utilization) and is highly effective in severe CCB toxicity. This can be given in combination with continued calcium and vasopressors.

Thai EM Board MCQs

Q1. A 62-year-old man with hypertension on amlodipine (a dihydropyridine) presents with symptomatic bradycardia and hypotension after an intentional overdose. Which clinical finding would be MOST helpful in distinguishing this from β-blocker toxicity?
  • A. Presence of wide QRS complex
  • B. Serum glucose is elevated (hyperglycemia)
  • C. Presence of seizures
  • D. Respiratory depression requiring intubation
Hyperglycemia is characteristic of CCB toxicity (due to inhibited insulin secretion) but hypoglycemia or euglycemia is more common with β-blockers. This is a key distinguishing feature between the two toxidromes.
Q2. A 38-year-old woman intentionally ingests sustained-release verapamil. Which type of calcium channel blocker property makes her toxicity more severe than if she had ingested diltiazem?
  • A. Verapamil is highly protein-bound limiting its elimination
  • B. Verapamil has intrinsic sympathomimetic activity
  • C. Verapamil has greater negative inotropic and chronotropic effects than diltiazem
  • D. Verapamil is hydrophilic and causes severe CNS toxicity
Verapamil is a non-dihydropyridine with strong negative inotropic and chronotropic effects (more potent depression of cardiac contractility and conduction). This makes it more cardiotoxic than diltiazem. While both are non-dihydropyridines, verapamil's effects are more pronounced, making it the most lethal CCB.
Q3. A patient with diltiazem toxicity receives high-dose insulin therapy and develops hypokalemia (K+ 2.9 mEq/L) during the infusion. What is the most appropriate management?
  • A. Administer IV potassium and continue insulin therapy with frequent K+ monitoring
  • B. Discontinue insulin therapy immediately
  • C. Give sodium polystyrene sulfonate to remove excess potassium
  • D. Give calcium to counteract hyperkalemia
Hypokalemia is an expected side effect of high-dose insulin therapy due to insulin-mediated intracellular shift of potassium. This requires potassium supplementation and frequent monitoring. The hypokalemia should be treated, but the insulin therapy should not be discontinued.
Q4. A 71-year-old male on nifedipine (dihydropyridine) for hypertension presents with syncope. On evaluation: HR 50 bpm, BP 82/56 mmHg, normal glucose, alert mental status. Compared to a patient with verapamil toxicity at the same vital sign parameters, which statement about nifedipine toxicity is correct?
  • A. Nifedipine causes more CNS toxicity than verapamil
  • B. Nifedipine requires higher doses of calcium than verapamil
  • C. Nifedipine causes more significant hyperglycemia than verapamil
  • D. Nifedipine generally causes less severe cardiac toxicity than verapamil due to greater selectivity for peripheral vasodilation
Nifedipine (a dihydropyridine) is more selective for vascular smooth muscle and causes peripheral vasodilation. In overdose, nifedipine typically causes less severe negative inotropic effects compared to non-dihydropyridines like verapamil. Therefore, nifedipine toxicity is generally less severe overall.

Thai EM Board — InTraining Exam MCQs

Q1. During management of severe verapamil toxicity with high-dose insulin therapy, you note the patient's glucose has dropped from 280 mg/dL to 65 mg/dL over 30 minutes. The patient is still in shock (BP 60/30, HR 35). What is the most appropriate action?
  • A. Administer insulin bolus to lower glucose further
  • B. Increase IV dextrose infusion to maintain glucose 100-200 mg/dL
  • C. Discontinue insulin due to severe hypoglycemia
  • D. Give subcutaneous glucagon for hypoglycemia
Euglycemia (not hypoglycemia) should be maintained during HIET. The dextrose infusion should be titrated to keep blood glucose in the 100-200 mg/dL range for optimal effect. Hypoglycemia should be corrected, and the dextrose infusion increased.

McGraw-Hill Specialty Board Review MCQs

Q1. Which statement best explains why nifedipine (a dihydropyridine) often causes reflex tachycardia at therapeutic doses, while verapamil (non-dihydropyridine) causes bradycardia?
  • A. Nifedipine has partial agonist activity at calcium channels
  • B. Verapamil has alpha-blocking activity that nifedipine lacks
  • C. Dihydropyridines are vascular-selective; non-dihydropyridines have direct nodal effects
  • D. Nifedipine is metabolized faster, preventing bradycardia development
Dihydropyridines like nifedipine are selective for peripheral vascular smooth muscle, causing vasodilation and reflex tachycardia to compensate. Non-dihydropyridines like verapamil have direct effects on the AV node and sinoatrial node, causing bradycardia and AV block. This selectivity explains the different cardiac effects between the two classes.
Q2. A patient with severe verapamil toxicity develops sudden onset of pulmonary edema despite treatment with inotropes and vasopressors. What is the most likely mechanism?
  • A. Excessive IV fluid administration during treatment
  • B. Decreased myocardial contractility from CCB leading to elevated LVEDP
  • C. Acute kidney injury from hypotension causing fluid retention
  • D. Sepsis complicating the overdose
Pulmonary edema in CCB toxicity results from decreased myocardial contractility (negative inotropy) leading to elevated left ventricular end-diastolic pressure and pulmonary capillary wedge pressure. Even with vasopressor support of blood pressure, the underlying myocardial dysfunction persists.
Q3. A 45-year-old man with diltiazem toxicity receives high-dose insulin therapy. Over 2 hours, his insulin infusion is increased to 1 unit/kg/hr and dextrose is titrated. His blood pressure improves from 50/30 to 88/52 mmHg. What is the mechanism of insulin's benefit in this setting?
  • A. Improved intracellular calcium handling and myocardial substrate utilization
  • B. Insulin blocks calcium channels preventing further toxicity
  • C. Insulin stimulates adrenaline release from the adrenal medulla
  • D. Insulin causes peripheral vasoconstriction improving blood pressure
High-dose insulin improves cardiac contractility through enhanced intracellular calcium handling (calcium-troponin interaction), improved myocardial substrate utilization (increased carbohydrate metabolism), and possibly enhanced calcium sensitization. This works independently of calcium channel function, bypassing the CCB-induced blockade.
Q4. A patient presenting with severe CCB toxicity is unresponsive to repeated calcium doses and escalating doses of vasopressors. Before considering ECMO, which other therapy has been successfully used in severe, refractory cases?
  • A. Glucagon infusion (glucagon blocks calcium channels)
  • B. Sodium bicarbonate for wide QRS dysrhythmias
  • C. Anticoagulation with heparin to prevent thromboembolism
  • D. Lipid emulsion (lipid rescue) therapy for severe refractory cases
Lipid emulsion (lipid rescue) therapy has been used successfully in severe, refractory CCB toxicity. The mechanism is thought to involve improved myocardial perfusion and substrate availability. While data is limited, case reports demonstrate efficacy in otherwise refractory cases before ECMO is needed.

End-of-Chapter Assessment: 20 Questions

Q1. A 52-year-old man ingests an unknown quantity of verapamil. He presents with HR 35 bpm, BP 68/38 mmHg, alert mental status, glucose 310 mg/dL, K+ 3.8 mEq/L. Which finding is MOST helpful in identifying this as CCB toxicity rather than β-blocker toxicity?
  • A. Bradycardia and hypotension
  • B. Alert mental status
  • C. Hyperglycemia (elevated serum glucose)
  • D. Normal serum potassium
Hyperglycemia (310 mg/dL) is characteristic of CCB toxicity. β-blocker toxicity more commonly causes hypoglycemia or euglycemia. The elevated glucose from CCB-induced suppression of insulin secretion is a key distinguishing feature.
Q2. A 67-year-old female with diltiazem toxicity receives 3 doses of calcium gluconate 10-15 mL IV without significant clinical improvement. Heart rate remains 38 bpm, BP 62/32 mmHg. What is the most appropriate next step?
  • A. Repeat calcium dosing every 10-15 minutes indefinitely
  • B. Start high-dose insulin (1 unit/kg IV) with dextrose infusion
  • C. Give epinephrine 1 mg IV for cardiac arrest
  • D. Call for ECMO preparation immediately
After initial calcium therapy without adequate response, high-dose insulin therapy should be initiated. HIET has proven efficacy in CCB toxicity that is unresponsive to calcium alone.
Q3. A patient with nifedipine (dihydropyridine) overdose presents with hypotension and reflex tachycardia (HR 125 bpm). Compared to verapamil toxicity, why is reflex tachycardia more likely with nifedipine?
  • A. Dihydropyridines are peripheral vascular-selective and cause reflex tachycardia; non-dihydropyridines have direct nodal effects
  • B. Nifedipine is more rapidly absorbed causing faster symptom onset
  • C. Nifedipine has intrinsic alpha-agonist activity
  • D. Verapamil causes complete AV block preventing all conduction
Nifedipine is a dihydropyridine that is selective for peripheral vascular smooth muscle, causing vasodilation and reflex tachycardia. Verapamil, a non-dihydropyridine, has direct negative chronotropic effects on the SA and AV nodes.
Q4. A 50-year-old woman with verapamil toxicity has received high-dose insulin therapy for 2 hours with improvement in blood pressure (now 95/55) but persistent bradycardia (HR 32 bpm). Her glucose is 180 mg/dL and K+ is 3.2 mEq/L. What is the most appropriate next intervention?
  • A. Increase insulin infusion to 2 units/kg/hour
  • B. Discontinue insulin and give glucagon for bradycardia
  • C. Give atropine 1-2 mg IV for bradycardia
  • D. Administer IV potassium supplementation and consider transcutaneous pacing if hemodynamically unstable
This patient has responded partially to insulin (improved BP) but remains bradycardic. The hypokalemia (3.2) should be corrected as it can worsen arrhythmias. After correcting potassium and continuing insulin, if bradycardia persists as a hemodynamic problem, pacing should be considered.
Q5. A patient with diltiazem toxicity develops pulmonary edema during treatment with vasopressors and high-dose insulin. What is the most appropriate intervention?
  • A. Administer more vasopressors to increase blood pressure
  • B. Give diuretics and consider positive pressure ventilation (CPAP/intubation) while continuing inotropic support
  • C. Fluid restriction and withhold dextrose infusion
  • D. Emergent intubation and sedation
Pulmonary edema in CCB toxicity results from myocardial dysfunction and elevated LVEDP. While vasopressors maintain blood pressure, they do not improve myocardial contractility. Adding diuretics (to reduce preload) and continuing inotropic therapy is appropriate.
Q6. A 58-year-old man with amlodipine (dihydropyridine) toxicity presents with hypotension (BP 55/28) but normal heart rate (80 bpm). Which statement best explains this unusual presentation?
  • A. Amlodipine simultaneously blocks both calcium channels and alpha-receptors
  • B. The patient has developed cardiogenic shock from myocardial depression
  • C. Dihydropyridines cause primarily peripheral vasodilation without significant negative chronotropic effects
  • D. The patient has concurrent beta-blocker toxicity unexpectedly complicating the presentation
Amlodipine, a dihydropyridine, is predominantly vascular-selective, causing peripheral vasodilation and hypotension without direct cardiac effects. At therapeutic doses, reflex tachycardia compensates. In severe overdose, vasodilation is profound but direct negative chronotropic effects are minimal, allowing maintained or normal heart rate.
Q7. A patient with verapamil toxicity has severe hypokalemia (K+ 2.5 mEq/L) during high-dose insulin therapy. ECG shows peaked T waves. What is the most appropriate management?
  • A. Administer sodium polystyrene sulfonate (Kayexalate) for hyperkalemia
  • B. Administer IV potassium replacement and correct metabolic acidosis with improved perfusion
  • C. Give calcium gluconate and insulin for hyperkalemia
  • D. Discontinue insulin therapy immediately due to severe electrolyte disturbance
Peaked T waves suggest hyperkalemia, but the patient has low potassium. The discordance suggests metabolic acidosis (from poor perfusion) which causes peaked T waves even with normal/low K+. Regardless, potassium should be repleted and metabolic acidosis should be corrected with improved perfusion.
Q8. Which clinical scenario is LEAST likely to represent severe calcium channel blocker toxicity requiring intensive intervention?
  • A. Bradycardia (HR 35) with hypotension (BP 50/25) and AV block
  • B. Progressive bradycardia with widening QRS and cardiogenic shock
  • C. Syncope with HR 30 bpm and second-degree AV block
  • D. Mild tachycardia (HR 100) with normal blood pressure and normal QRS after nifedipine ingestion
Asymptomatic or mildly symptomatic patients with stable vital signs do not require intensive intervention. Severe CCB toxicity presents with bradycardia, hypotension/shock, and AV conduction abnormalities. A patient with mild tachycardia and normal blood pressure does not fit the typical presentation.
Q9. A patient with diltiazem toxicity initially responds to calcium therapy with improved heart rate and blood pressure. However, 4 hours later, symptoms recur with recurrent bradycardia and hypotension. What is the most likely mechanism?
  • A. Continued absorption from sustained-release formulation overwhelming initial calcium effect
  • B. Development of calcium channel resistance from tachyphylaxis
  • C. Progression to complete AV block from disease progression
  • D. Myocardial infarction complicating the toxicity
Recurrent or biphasic toxicity can occur as sustained-release formulations continue to be absorbed. The initial calcium dose may have worn off or new drug absorption may be overwhelming the effect. Sustained-release CCBs can cause delayed symptom onset and prolonged toxicity.
Q10. A 44-year-old with severe verapamil toxicity is on maximal medical therapy (calcium, high-dose insulin, vasopressors, atropine) yet remains in profound cardiogenic shock with BP 45/20 and HR 28. The team is considering ECMO. Which other therapy could be attempted before ECMO?
  • A. Repeat boluses of atropine to maximum 10 mg
  • B. Administer methylene blue for myocardial toxicity
  • C. Initiate lipid emulsion (lipid rescue) therapy as bridging therapy
  • D. Add dantrolene for suspected neuroleptic malignant syndrome
Lipid emulsion therapy has been successfully used in severe, refractory CCB toxicity. Case reports demonstrate reversal of refractory shock after lipid rescue. While evidence is limited, it represents a bridging therapy before ECMO.
Q11. Which of the following best describes the therapeutic window for pralidoxime (2-PAM) effectiveness in CCB toxicity?
  • A. Pralidoxime is NOT indicated in CCB toxicity; it has no mechanism of action in this poisoning
  • B. Pralidoxime is effective only if given within 30 minutes of CCB ingestion
  • C. Pralidoxime should be given as first-line therapy in CCB toxicity
  • D. Pralidoxime is a second-line agent for vasopressor-refractory CCB toxicity
Unlike organophosphate poisoning (where pralidoxime is a key antidote that works by reactivating acetylcholinesterase), pralidoxime has no role in CCB toxicity. CCBs do not inhibit acetylcholinesterase. Calcium, insulin, and vasopressors are the indicated therapies for CCB poisoning.
Q12. A 45-year-old with extended-release nifedipine toxicity is asymptomatic at 6 hours post-ingestion with normal vital signs. Which is the most appropriate management?
  • A. Discharge home after 6 hours observation since currently asymptomatic
  • B. Continue hospitalization and observation for 12-24 hours total due to ER formulation delayed toxicity
  • C. Give activated charcoal now and discharge if repeat vital signs normal at 12 hours
  • D. Perform cardiac catheterization to rule out coronary ischemia
Extended-release CCB formulations can delay toxicity onset to 6-12 hours or longer after ingestion. An asymptomatic patient at 6 hours post-ER ingestion must be observed for 12-24 hours total. Premature discharge risks missing delayed toxicity development and cardiogenic shock.
Q13. A child accidentally ingests a single verapamil tablet from a medication bottle. Which statement regarding pediatric CCB toxicity is most accurate?
  • A. Single tablet ingestion in children is always benign; home observation sufficient
  • B. All pediatric CCB ingestions require medical attention and observation; deaths reported after single-tablet ingestion
  • C. Children require higher doses of calcium per kg than adults
  • D. Pediatric CCB toxicity is always less severe than adult toxicity
Children may be sensitive to CCB toxicity, and deaths have been reported after even single-tablet ingestion. Therefore, all pediatric CCB ingestions should be referred for medical attention and observation, regardless of the quantity ingested.
Q14. A 52-year-old woman presents 3 hours after ingesting 30 tablets of amlodipine. Her BP is 70/40 mmHg and HR is 110 bpm. IV calcium and glucagon have not improved her hemodynamics. Which intervention has demonstrated the most consistent efficacy for refractory CCB-induced cardiogenic shock?
  • A. Dopamine infusion at 20 mcg/kg/min
  • B. High-dose insulin euglycemia (1 unit/kg bolus + infusion)
  • C. Repeat calcium chloride 1g IV every 20 minutes
  • D. Sodium bicarbonate 2 mEq/kg IV bolus
High-dose insulin euglycemia therapy (HIE) with 1 unit/kg bolus followed by 0.5–2 units/kg/hour infusion has emerged as the most effective intervention for CCB-induced cardiogenic shock refractory to conventional therapy. Insulin improves cardiac glucose metabolism and calcium handling independent of adrenergic signaling. Dextrose infusion and potassium replacement are mandatory adjuncts.
Q15. A patient with CCB overdose becomes refractory to pharmacologic treatment and requires mechanical circulatory support. Which device is most appropriate as a bridge to recovery?
  • A. Intra-aortic balloon pump (IABP)
  • B. Veno-venous ECMO (VV-ECMO)
  • C. Veno-arterial ECMO (VA-ECMO)
  • D. Impella device only
Veno-arterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (VA-ECMO) provides complete cardiopulmonary bypass support for patients with refractory CCB-induced cardiogenic shock, allowing time for drug metabolism and cardiac recovery. It should be considered early in patients who fail pharmacologic therapy including calcium, glucagon, and high-dose insulin.
Q16. Which laboratory finding is characteristic of significant CCB toxicity and reflects impaired insulin secretion from pancreatic beta cells?
  • A. Hyperglycemia
  • B. Hypoglycemia
  • C. Hyperkalemia
  • D. Metabolic alkalosis
Hyperglycemia is a hallmark of significant CCB toxicity. Calcium channel blockers inhibit L-type calcium channels in pancreatic beta cells, preventing insulin release and causing glucose elevation. The degree of hyperglycemia correlates with toxicity severity and can serve as a prognostic marker. This is also why exogenous high-dose insulin therapy is particularly beneficial.
Q17. A 68-year-old man presents with bradycardia (HR 38), hypotension (BP 80/50), and PR prolongation on ECG after verapamil ingestion. After atropine and calcium chloride fail, glucagon 5 mg IV is given. What is the primary mechanism of glucagon's benefit in CCB toxicity?
  • A. Directly opens L-type calcium channels blocked by CCB
  • B. Increases cAMP via beta-adrenergic-independent receptor pathway
  • C. Competitively displaces CCB from calcium channel receptor
  • D. Increases intracellular calcium through Na-Ca exchange
Glucagon increases intracellular cAMP through a G-protein coupled receptor pathway that is independent of the beta-adrenergic receptor blocked by CCBs. This cAMP increase activates protein kinase A, which phosphorylates L-type calcium channels and improves cardiac inotropy and chronotropy. The effect is independent of CCB receptor binding.
Q18. A patient with severe verapamil overdose requires whole bowel irrigation. Which preparation is used and what is the primary indication?
  • A. Polyethylene glycol electrolyte solution to flush sustained-release tablets
  • B. Activated charcoal repeated every 4 hours to bind released drug
  • C. Sodium phosphate enema to stimulate intestinal motility
  • D. Sorbitol 70% solution for osmotic catharsis
Polyethylene glycol electrolyte solution (PEG-ELS) is used for whole bowel irrigation at 1–2 L/hour (adults) via nasogastric tube. It is indicated for massive sustained-release CCB ingestions to reduce absorption by mechanically flushing unabsorbed drug through the gastrointestinal tract before systemic absorption occurs. It is particularly important for sustained-release formulations due to their prolonged drug release profile.
Q19. Which of the following CCB overdose patients most likely requires ICU admission for at least 24 hours of monitoring?
  • A. Adult who ingested 1 tablet of regular-release amlodipine 5 mg
  • B. Child who ingested 1 tablet of regular-release nifedipine 10 mg and is asymptomatic
  • C. Adult who took a therapeutic dose of diltiazem and has normal vitals at 6 hours
  • D. Adult who ingested extended-release verapamil 240 mg tablets, currently asymptomatic at 4 hours
Extended-release (ER) verapamil formulations release drug over 12–24 hours, meaning patients may initially appear well but develop severe cardiovascular toxicity later. Any ingestion of a sustained-release CCB formulation requires at minimum 24 hours of cardiac monitoring regardless of initial presentation. Immediate-release formulations in small doses in adults may be safely observed for shorter periods.
Q20. A patient with CCB toxicity is given calcium chloride 1g IV. Which statement about calcium administration in CCB overdose is correct?
  • A. Calcium is contraindicated as it can cause dangerous hypercalcemia
  • B. Calcium gluconate and calcium chloride contain equal elemental calcium
  • C. Calcium chloride contains approximately 3x more elemental calcium than calcium gluconate
  • D. Calcium completely reverses the L-type calcium channel blockade
Calcium chloride contains approximately 3 times more elemental calcium per gram than calcium gluconate (270 mg vs 90 mg elemental calcium per gram). Both can be used, but calcium chloride is preferred in severe toxicity for rapid effect. Calcium does not reverse the block completely but can improve cardiac contractility by increasing the calcium gradient. Large doses may be required (10 grams or more reported in some cases).
